questions.q: A pharmacy chain in Samarkand loses money because medicines expire on the shelves and nobody knows the stock level in each branch. The Chief Operating Officer wants a central inventory system before the new branch opens in March. Write a system request with all 5 elements.
questions.a:
ElementAnswer
Project sponsorChief Operating Officer
Business needReduce losses from expired medicines; know the stock level in every branch
Business requirementsReal-time stock view for all branches; expiry-date alerts; automatic reorder suggestions; monthly stock reports
Business valueExpired stock down by 50%; about $40,000 saved per year; 1 fewer stock clerk
Special issues or constraintsMust be ready before the new branch opens in March; must work with the existing cash registers

Check: requirements are capabilities (what it does), value is measurable (what we gain).

questions.q:
Classify each change as Business Process Automation, Improvement or Reengineering:
1) A bank replaces paper deposit slips with a tablet form; the steps stay the same.
2) A bookshop closes all its stores and becomes an online-only seller.
3) A clinic studies its patient check-in process, removes two approval steps and adds online pre-registration.
4) A warehouse uses barcode scanners instead of writing item codes by hand.
5) A taxi company stops owning cars and becomes a platform that connects drivers and passengers.
6) A university redesigns its course-approval workflow so that the dean signs electronically and one meeting is dropped.
questions.a:
1) Automation (technology replaces manual work, same process) · 2) Reengineering (completely new way of doing business) · 3) Improvement (study and redesign the process) · 4) Automation · 5) Reengineering · 6) Improvement.

Rule: same steps but faster = BPA; redesigned steps = BPI; the old way is obliterated = BPR (risky, rare, needs top management support).

questions.q:
In a system request for a hotel booking system, which item is a business value (not a business requirement)?
A) Online room search by date and price
B) A 5% increase in room occupancy
C) Management reports on daily bookings
D) The system must be ready before the tourist season
questions.a: B, because business value is the measurable benefit for the organization; A and C are capabilities (business requirements) and D is a special issue or constraint.

questions.q: Define business process management (BPM). Give its 3 benefits and list the business analyst's 4 steps in BPM.
questions.a:
BPM = a methodology used to continuously improve end-to-end business processes, inside the organization and across business partners.

Benefits: (1) more agility, (2) better alignment with industry best practices, (3) more efficiency (costs found and removed).

  1. Define and map the steps of a process.
  2. Improve the steps that add value.
  3. Remove or merge the steps that do not add value.
  4. Create or adjust electronic workflows to match the improved process (this is where IS projects are most often found).

questions.q: Depict graphically: how a project goes from a business need to the approval decision.
questions.a: Key labels: business need (opportunity or pain) → high-level business requirements + business value → project sponsor → system request (5 elements) → feasibility analysis (technical, economic, organizational) → approval (steering) committee → go / no-go.
questions.diagram:
flowchart LR
  N(["Business need: opportunity or pain"]) --> R["Business requirements + business value"]
  R --> S[Project sponsor]
  S --> SR["System request: 5 elements"]
  SR --> F["Feasibility analysis: technical, economic, organizational"]
  F --> C{"Approval committee"}
  C -->|go| P([Project starts])
  C -->|no-go| X([Rejected])

questions.q: Sort into development cost, operational cost, tangible benefit or intangible benefit: hardware upgrades; data conversion costs; development team salaries; increased sales; increased market share; higher quality products; reductions in staff; operational team salaries; office space and equipment; software upgrades.
questions.a:
Development (Year 0)Operational (every year)Tangible benefitIntangible benefit
Data conversion costs
Development team salaries
Office space and equipment		Hardware upgrades
Operational team salaries
Software upgrades		Increased sales
Reductions in staff		Increased market share
Higher quality products

Test: paid once to build = development; paid every year to run = operational. Sales (money) is tangible; market share is intangible.

questions.q: A bank's IT team has only built websites. Now they must build a mobile banking app with loans, cards and payments at once, and connect it to a 20-year-old core banking system. Assess the technical feasibility using the 4 risk factors.
questions.a:
• Familiarity with the application: they never built mobile banking → higher risk.
  • Familiarity with the technology: new to mobile development → higher risk.
  • Project size: loans + cards + payments at once = large → higher risk.
  • Compatibility: hard to integrate with an old core system → higher risk.

Conclusion: technical risk is high on all 4 factors. Reduce it with training or hiring experienced developers, and by splitting the project into smaller parts.

questions.q:
Which of these is NOT a technical feasibility risk factor?
A) Project size
B) Compatibility with existing technology
C) Strategic alignment with the business
D) Familiarity with the technology
questions.a: C, because strategic alignment is used to assess organizational feasibility; the technical factors are familiarity with the application and technology, project size and compatibility.

questions.q: Who receives the system request and the feasibility analysis? What two jobs does feasibility analysis do, and what may the committee ask the analyst to prepare?
questions.a:
The information systems approval committee (steering committee); it decides whether the project should be undertaken.

Two jobs: (1) guide the go / no-go decision; (2) identify the important risks to manage if the project is approved.

The committee may ask for a more detailed business case.

questions.q:
Complete: "The more expensive the project, the more ______ the economic feasibility analysis should be."
A) optimistic
B) detailed
C) informal
D) short
questions.a: B, because money is limited and many projects compete for it, so expensive projects need a more detailed cost–benefit analysis.

questions.q: Depict graphically: the 4 steps of an economic feasibility analysis and the measures used in the last step.
questions.a: Key labels: (1) identify costs and benefits (one-time and recurring) → (2) assign values (even intangibles if possible) → (3) determine cash flow (usually 3–5 years) → (4) assess economic value with ROI, BEP and NPV.
questions.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A["1. Identify costs and benefits"] --> B["2. Assign values"]
  B --> C["3. Determine cash flow: 3 to 5 years"]
  C --> D["4. Assess economic value"]
  D --> R[ROI]
  D --> P["BEP: payback"]
  D --> N[NPV]

questions.q:
During Project Planning phase, next cash flows were identified:

Development costs: Consultant fees $35 000; Hardware and software $55 000; Data conversion tools $15 000
Operational costs: Software licensing fees $12 000; Hardware repairs $8 000; User training $5 000
Tangible benefits: Increased sales $40 000; Reduction in staff $20 000; Reductions in IT costs $5 000

Find: ROI, BEP and NPV, if project life cycle is 3 years and rate of return = 5%.
questions.a:
Assumption: development costs are one-time in Year 0; operating costs and benefits are annual in Years 1–3.

Development (Year 0) = 35,000 + 55,000 + 15,000 = 105,000. Operational = 12,000 + 8,000 + 5,000 = 25,000 per year. Benefits = 40,000 + 20,000 + 5,000 = 65,000 per year.

Year 0Year 1Year 2Year 3Total
Total Benefits–65,00065,00065,000195,000
Total Costs105,00025,00025,00025,000180,000
Net Benefits(105,000)40,00040,00040,00015,000
Cumulative(105,000)(65,000)(25,000)15,000
Divide by (1.05)n11.051.10251.157625
PV of Benefits–61,904.7658,956.9256,149.44177,011.12
PV of Costs105,000.0023,809.5222,675.7421,595.94173,081.20

ROI = (Total Benefits − Total Costs) / Total Costs = (195,000 − 180,000) / 180,000 = 15,000 / 180,000 = 8.33%

BEP: the cumulative first turns positive in Year 3, so 2 negative years (Year 0 is not counted). BEP = 2 + (40,000 − 15,000) / 40,000 = 2 + 25,000 / 40,000 = 2 + 0.625 = 2.63 years

NPV = Σ PV of Benefits − Σ PV of Costs = 177,011.12 − 173,081.20 = $3,929.92. NPV > 0 → the project is economically acceptable.

Quick check (same net every year): −105,000 + 40,000 × 2.723248 = 3,929.92 ✓

questions.q:
During Project Planning phase, next cash flows were identified (not grouped, classify them yourself):

Development team salaries: $60 000
Software upgrades: $10 000
Increased sales: $50 000
Vendor installation: $20 000
Communications charges: $5 000
Increased brand recognition: (no dollar value could be estimated)
Office space and equipment: $10 000
Better supplier prices: $20 000
Operational team salaries: $15 000

(a) Find: ROI, BEP and NPV, if project life cycle is 3 years and rate of return = 20%. Should the project be accepted?
(b) Would your decision change if the rate of return were 10%?
questions.a:
Assumption: development costs are one-time in Year 0; operating costs and benefits are annual in Years 1–3.

Classify first: Development (Year 0) = development team salaries 60,000 + vendor installation 20,000 + office space and equipment 10,000 = 90,000. Operational (every year) = software upgrades 10,000 + communications charges 5,000 + operational team salaries 15,000 = 30,000. Tangible benefits (every year) = increased sales 50,000 + better supplier prices 20,000 = 70,000. Increased brand recognition is an intangible benefit with no dollar value, so it stays out of the table (mention it in the conclusion).

Year 0Year 1Year 2Year 3Total
Total Benefits–70,00070,00070,000210,000
Total Costs90,00030,00030,00030,000180,000
Net Benefits(90,000)40,00040,00040,00030,000
Cumulative(90,000)(50,000)(10,000)30,000
Divide by (1.20)n11.21.441.728
PV of Benefits–58,333.3348,611.1140,509.26147,453.70
PV of Costs90,000.0025,000.0020,833.3317,361.11153,194.44

ROI = (Total Benefits − Total Costs) / Total Costs = (210,000 − 180,000) / 180,000 = 30,000 / 180,000 = 16.67%

BEP: the cumulative first turns positive in Year 3, so 2 negative years (Year 0 is not counted). BEP = 2 + (40,000 − 30,000) / 40,000 = 2 + 10,000 / 40,000 = 2 + 0.25 = 2.25 years

NPV = Σ PV of Benefits − Σ PV of Costs = 147,453.70 − 153,194.44 = ($5,740.74), negative. NPV < 0 → the project should not be accepted.

Conclusion: ROI is positive and the BEP is inside the 3-year life, so the "naïve" measures look good. But the more rigorous NPV is negative at 20%, so the project should not be accepted. (The intangible brand recognition can be mentioned to the committee, but it does not change the numbers.)

(b) At 10%: PV of Benefits = 174,079.64; PV of Costs = 164,605.56; NPV = $9,474.08 > 0 → acceptable. The decision flips because a lower rate discounts future benefits less. NPV = 0 at about 15.9%, so the rate must be below about 15.9% for a positive NPV.

questions.q:
During Project Planning phase, next cash flows were identified for a café chain's mobile ordering app:

Development costs: Hardware and software $80 000; Consultant fees $30 000
Operational costs: Software licensing fees $15 000 per year; Hardware repairs $5 000 in Year 1, $7 000 in Year 2, $10 000 in Year 3
Tangible benefits: Increased sales $45 000 in Year 1, $55 000 in Year 2, $70 000 in Year 3; Reductions in inventory $15 000 per year

Find: ROI, BEP and NPV, if project life cycle is 3 years and rate of return = 10%. Is the project economically acceptable?
questions.a:
Assumption: development costs are one-time in Year 0; operating costs and benefits are annual in Years 1–3.

Development (Year 0) = 80,000 + 30,000 = 110,000. Operational: Year 1 = 15,000 + 5,000 = 20,000; Year 2 = 15,000 + 7,000 = 22,000; Year 3 = 15,000 + 10,000 = 25,000. Benefits: Year 1 = 45,000 + 15,000 = 60,000; Year 2 = 55,000 + 15,000 = 70,000; Year 3 = 70,000 + 15,000 = 85,000.

The yearly amounts are different here (growth), so every year is discounted separately. The quick shortcut with one net amount does not work.

Year 0Year 1Year 2Year 3Total
Total Benefits–60,00070,00085,000215,000
Total Costs110,00020,00022,00025,000177,000
Net Benefits(110,000)40,00048,00060,00038,000
Cumulative(110,000)(70,000)(22,000)38,000
Divide by (1.10)n11.11.211.331
PV of Benefits–54,545.4557,851.2463,861.76176,258.45
PV of Costs110,000.0018,181.8218,181.8218,782.87165,146.51

ROI = (Total Benefits − Total Costs) / Total Costs = (215,000 − 177,000) / 177,000 = 38,000 / 177,000 = 21.47%

BEP: the cumulative first turns positive in Year 3, so 2 negative years (Year 0 is not counted). BEP = 2 + (60,000 − 38,000) / 60,000 = 2 + 22,000 / 60,000 = 2 + 0.367 = 2.37 years

NPV = Σ PV of Benefits − Σ PV of Costs = 176,258.45 − 165,146.51 = $11,111.95 (from the rounded totals: 11,111.94). NPV > 0 → the project is economically acceptable.

questions.q:
During Project Planning phase, next cash flows were identified:

Development costs: Office space and equipment $25 000; Vendor installation $30 000; Data conversion tools $15 000
Operational costs: Software licensing fees $10 000; Hardware upgrades $10 000; User training $5 000
Tangible benefits: Increased sales $45 000; Reductions in inventory $20 000; Reduction in staff $25 000

Find: ROI, BEP and NPV, if project life cycle is 3 years and rate of return = 15%.
questions.a:
Assumption: development costs are one-time in Year 0; operating costs and benefits are annual in Years 1–3.

Development (Year 0) = 25,000 + 30,000 + 15,000 = 70,000. Operational = 10,000 + 10,000 + 5,000 = 25,000 per year. Benefits = 45,000 + 20,000 + 25,000 = 90,000 per year.

Year 0Year 1Year 2Year 3Total
Total Benefits–90,00090,00090,000270,000
Total Costs70,00025,00025,00025,000145,000
Net Benefits(70,000)65,00065,00065,000125,000
Cumulative(70,000)(5,000)60,000125,000
Divide by (1.15)n11.151.32251.520875
PV of Benefits–78,260.8768,052.9359,176.46205,490.26
PV of Costs70,000.0021,739.1318,903.5916,437.91127,080.63

ROI = (Total Benefits − Total Costs) / Total Costs = (270,000 − 145,000) / 145,000 = 125,000 / 145,000 = 86.21%

BEP: the cumulative first turns positive in Year 2, so 1 negative year (Year 0 is not counted). BEP = 1 + (65,000 − 60,000) / 65,000 = 1 + 5,000 / 65,000 = 1 + 0.077 = 1.08 years

NPV = Σ PV of Benefits − Σ PV of Costs = 205,490.26 − 127,080.63 = $78,409.63. NPV > 0 → the project is economically acceptable.

Quick check (same net every year): −70,000 + 65,000 × 2.283225 = 78,409.63 ✓

questions.q:
During Project Planning phase, next cash flows were identified:

Development team salaries $40 000; Hardware repairs $15 000; Increased sales $30 000; User training $10 000; Data conversion costs $10 000; Reductions in IT costs $15 000; Improved customer service (no dollar value).

Find the year when the cumulative net cash flow turns positive, and the BEP (project life 3 years).
questions.a:
Classify: Development (Year 0) = 40,000 + 10,000 = 50,000. Operational every year = hardware repairs 15,000 + user training 10,000 = 25,000. Benefits every year = 30,000 + 15,000 = 45,000. Improved customer service is intangible, left out.

Year 0Year 1Year 2Year 3
Net Benefits(50,000)20,00020,00020,000
Cumulative(50,000)(30,000)(10,000)10,000

The cumulative turns positive in Year 3. BEP = 2 + (20,000 − 10,000) / 20,000 = 2 + 10,000 / 20,000 = 2.50 years.

Trap: if you put hardware repairs and user training in Year 0, you get (75,000) → (30,000) → 15,000 → 60,000 and the wrong answer Year 2. Both are operational (recurring) costs.

questions.q:
A project has ROI = 12% and BEP = 2.4 years over a 3-year life, but NPV at the required rate is −$3,000. What should the analyst recommend?
A) Accept, because ROI is positive
B) Accept, because the BEP is inside the project life
C) Do not accept, because NPV < 0
D) Accept, because two of the three measures are positive
questions.a: C, because ROI and BEP are "naïve" and ignore the time value of money; NPV is the more rigorous and financially correct measure, and NPV < 0 means the project should not be accepted.

questions.q:
Which stakeholder group (champion, organizational management, system users) is each action aimed at?
1) Give them official roles on the project team.
2) Build a prototype to show the value to the executives who will benefit.
3) Market the benefits with memos and newsletters.
4) Hold weekly meetings to get their feedback.
5) Ask the champion to talk to his or her peers.
6) Give them specific tasks with deadlines.
questions.a: 1) System users · 2) Champion · 3) Organizational management · 4) System users · 5) Organizational management · 6) System users.

questions.q: A supermarket chain plans a new in-store stock system. The company strategy is growth through online sales. The only champion is the Head of IT, who will retire in two months. Store managers, who will use the system every day, were not consulted. Assess the organizational feasibility and suggest actions.
questions.a:
• Strategic alignment is weak: the system does not support the online-sales strategy → more risk. Action: show how stock data also supports online orders.
  • Single champion who is leaving: support (time, money, political support) may leave too. Action: find a new high-level champion, ideally more than one.
  • Users ignored: users decide success by using or not using the system. Action: give store managers official roles, tasks with deadlines and regular feedback meetings.
  • Present the benefits to management to secure the budget.

Conclusion: organizational feasibility is currently low.

questions.q:
The project champion is:
A) always the project manager
B) a high-level executive, usually but not always the project sponsor
C) the most experienced system user
D) the chair of the approval committee
questions.a: B, because the champion is a high-level executive who gives time, resources and political support, and is usually (not always) the project sponsor.

questions.q: Compare the three feasibility dimensions: the question each one answers and how each one is assessed.
questions.a:
DimensionQuestionHow assessed
TechnicalCan we build it?Risk factors: familiarity with application and technology, project size, compatibility
EconomicShould we build it? (Will it provide business value?)Cost–benefit analysis: cash flow → ROI, BEP, NPV
OrganizationalIf we build it, will they come? (Will it be used?)Strategic alignment + stakeholder analysis

questions.q: Depict graphically: how organizational feasibility is assessed, with the three most important stakeholders and their roles.
questions.a: Key labels: two ways, strategic alignment (more fit = less risk) and stakeholder analysis. Stakeholders: champion (initiates, promotes, gives time and resources), organizational management (knows the project, budgets money, encourages use), system users (decisions, hands-on work, decide success by using the system).
questions.diagram:
flowchart TD
  O(["Organizational feasibility"]) --> SA["Strategic alignment: more fit = less risk"]
  O --> ST[Stakeholder analysis]
  ST --> CH["Champion: initiates, promotes, time and resources"]
  ST --> MG["Management: knows project, budgets money, encourages use"]
  ST --> US["Users: decisions, hands-on work, decide success"]
